title: MANDEL: Should cop go on trial for not stopping High Park suicide?
article: A desperate teen was about to take his life. And a cop turned the other way.
Is that criminal, as the Crown contends? Or simply laziness and a job performance issue, as his lawyer argues?

When Toronto Police Const. Kyle Upjohn ignored a plea to save a young man about to commit suicide in High Park in 2016, lying and telling the concerned citizen who implored him for help that he was already on a call, he may have neglected his duty but there was no nefarious motive, lawyer Gary Clewley told the Ontario Court of Appeal.
And so he deserves to be hauled before the police tribunal, not a court of law.
"There's nothing here but neglect," Clewley said.
"Neglect and deceit. And as long as the deceit is designed to mask the neglect - 'I'm busy' - that's not enough."
Not enough to warrant a criminal charge of breach of trust by a public officer.
That was the charge Upjohn had been facing until it was quashed earlier this year by Ontario Superior Court Justice Maureen Forestell.
She found the law on breach of trust required evidence of a corrupt or dishonest ulterior motive for avoiding his duty.

Upjohn may have "put his own comfort or needs before the good of the public," but this was "not enough" evidence to prove an ulterior motive that is the basis of a breach of trust charge, the judge ruled.
The Crown was at the appeal court Wednesday to urge the panel to overturn her ruling and reinstate Upjohn's committal to stand trial.
"It was a duty that went to life and death," insisted Crown attorney Milan Rupic.
"He deliberately avoided doing his duty for a person he understood was about to hang himself."
On Feb. 2, 2016 at around 1:30 p.m., a woman walking in High Park came upon a young man throwing a rope over the branch of a tree. She ran to get help from a park staff person, but without success.
She then called her husband.

When he arrived at High Park, he spotted Upjohn in a marked police car and begged him to come and save the suicidal man. According to Forestell's summary of the case, Upjohn lied and said he was on a call.
He told the man to contact 911 and then drove away.
The concerned citizen found 19-year-old Alexandre Boucher in the park and cut him down from the tree. But it was too late.
He called 911 - and among those who responded was Upjohn.

The officer originally faced charges of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life but those were dropped by the Crown when the time of death couldn't be determined. Upjohn was then charged with breach of trust - usually laid when an official is accused of breaching his responsibilities as a public official.
Rupic told the appeal court Upjohn should stand trial for choosing to neglect his duty for personal gain: avoiding the "unpleasant work of dealing with a dead body."
The dubious judges asked the Crown whether any officer who neglected his duty should then face breach of trust charges.
Rupic said only "grave and serious" cases deserve criminal sanction.
Upjohn "was negligent in the execution of his duty and lied about why he did not do his job," conceded Clewley in his factum filed with the court.
"For this he will face the proper discipline consequences from his police service."
A 10-year veteran at the time, Upjohn has been suspended with pay since May 2016 and faces neglect of duty charges under the Police Services Act.
"What he did not do," continued the lawyer, "was misuse his public office for personal gain or for another prohibited purpose."

According to a Supreme Court decision known as Boulanger, breach of trust is designed for misfeasance and corruption, Clewley said, "not criminalizing public officials who do not do their jobs or who are bad at doing their jobs."
There's little doubt this cold-hearted officer failed badly to serve and protect that day.
And the horrible irony is this: the teen he ignored was a first year Criminal Justice student at Humber College. Had he hoped to be a police officer himself one day?
The appeal court has reserved its decision.
